topics: SLO targets: p95/p99 for TTFT and p95/p99 for per-token latency
Workload sizing: request size distributions, concurrency, burst patterns
Measurement plan: sampling, synthetic vs replay, significance and sample size
Security and deployment constraints: VPC, SOC2, KMS
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58 mins | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leo (Redwood SE), Sofia (Head of ML, HelioHealth), Raj (Infra), Mei (PM)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call and then we want to align on the POC charter — mainly the latency SLOs, sampling plan for benchmarks, and a realistic timeline.
[00:18] Sofia: Thanks Maya. We're mainly evaluating whether Redwood can meet our TTFT and per-token p95/p99s under our production-like traffic. We're also tight on cost so TPOT matters.
[00:30] Leo: Great. To be explicit, when I say TTFT I mean the time from request ingress to the first token emitted; TPOT we're using as total per-token average/percentile across generation. We'll walk through how we measure both.
[00:45] Raj: Quick network note — our infra requires VPC peering for any private deployment and egress must go through our proxy; that's going to shape the pilot.
[00:54] Maya: Noted. We'll add network checklist. First high-level question: what SLOs are you targeting today?
[01:05] Sofia: For conversational flows, business wants p95 TTFT < 250ms and p99 < 600ms for short replies (~40 tokens). For long-form completions we care more about TPOT — target p95 per-token latency ~30ms, and p99 under 60ms. These are ballpark.
[01:22] Leo: Okay. Those are aggressive for some open models but feasible with batching and prefix caching. We need to pick representative payloads — short question (<=40 tokens), medium (100 tokens), and long (500+ tokens) to exercise KV cache and attention stalls.
[01:38] Mei: We also need to define acceptable variance: e.g., during 5% traffic spikes it's okay to have degraded p99 by 20% if throughput is maintained, but we'd like graceful fallbacks.
[01:48] Maya: Good product constraint. We'll capture that in the SLO charter as an allowed degradation clause and fallback policy.

[02:10] Leo: On measurement approach: we recommend two complementary runs — a synthetic microbenchmark for controlled TTFT vs TPOT comparisons and a production-replay run using sampled historical traces to validate end-to-end behavior (network, marshalling, auth).
[02:25] Raj: How do you handle request shaping for replay? We have daily traffic with diurnal patterns and occasional 10x bursts.
[02:33] Leo: We'll stitch traffic slices: baseline (median weekday traffic), peak (90th percentile spikes captured over 3 weeks), and a synthetic burst test. Stitching ensures we capture both steady-state and tail behavior.
[02:45] Sofia: How large do you need the sample to get stable p99 estimates? p99 is noisy.
[02:51] Leo: For reliable p99 we like at least 10k effective samples per traffic slice after deduping. For production replay that's usually a 24–72 hour window depending on traffic volume. Statistical note: if events are correlated we might need more; we'll calculate confidence intervals in the measurement sheet.

[03:20] Maya: Let's talk instrumentation. We will ask Redwood to provide a benchmark script that emits both raw timing and structured events (ingress timestamp, service receive, model start, first-token, token emit times). That lets us compute TTFT, token-by-token deltas, and end-to-end TPOT.
[03:40] Leo: Right. We'll ship a small collector that writes traces to s3 in JSONL. We'll include sample size, sampling strategy, and an example collation notebook so your team can reproduce the metrics locally.

[04:05] Raj: Security — we need SOC 2 evidence, KMS integration for keys, and audit logs. If we do a private deployment, will Redwood's control plane still need access to logs?
[04:16] Maya: For Private deployments the control plane can be configured to be customer-managed; logs can stay in your account, and KMS/HSM can manage keys. We'll share our security pack after the call.
[04:28] Mei: Also can you surface per-request cost estimates so we can tie TTFT/TPOT tradeoffs to dollars?
[04:34] Leo: Yes, we'll add token-level cost breakdown and a cost delta table for different batching and quantization configurations.

[05:05] Sofia: On model variants: we may run a quantized 4-bit variant for TPOT-sensitive endpoints and a full model for high-quality paths. How do you compare across variants?
[05:14] Leo: We'll run side-by-side synthetic benchmarks using identical seeds and prompts to compare quality/perf. For POC acceptance we'll define a quality regression threshold using a small eval set you provide (we recommend ~200 prompts across intents).
[05:27] Sofia: Acceptable — we'll prepare the eval prompts.

[05:50] Maya: Acceptance criteria proposal: 1) For short-chat endpoint: p95 TTFT <= 250ms and p99 <= 600ms on the baseline traffic slice; 2) For long form: p95 per-token latency <= 30ms and p99 <= 60ms; 3) No more than 2% increase in error rate vs baseline; 4) Cost per 1k tokens within agreed delta. Any objections?
[06:12] Raj: Just clarify error rate definition — 5xx vs timeouts.
[06:16] Leo: We'll define error rate as 5xx + timeouts in the measurement workbook and show counts per slice.

[06:40] Sofia: How long is the POC? We were thinking 3 weeks.
[06:44] Maya: We recommend a 4-week engagement: week 0 prep (data export, infra setup), week 1 synthetic benchmarks and smoke runs, week 2 production replay and iterative tuning, week 3 final measurement and acceptance. But can compress to 3 weeks if resources are prioritized.
[06:57] Mei: We prefer 3 weeks. Is there a risk we won't get to replay in week 2?
[07:02] Leo: If network peering or security approval delays occur, we can run a closed-loop synthetic replay that mimics your trace distribution while waiting for peering. But for final acceptance we want a true replay.

[07:25] Maya: Let's cover sampling and significance quickly: for p95 you need fewer samples, but p99 is sensitive. We'll compute bootstrap CIs; we'll also check for non-stationarity in traffic (e.g., time-of-day spikes) and report per-window percentiles.
[07:40] Leo: Also important: tokenization variance. If you have many short-turn conversations, the per-token distribution may shift. Our scripts will annotate token counts so you can break down metrics by token-length bucket.

[08:05] Raj: Network egress — during replay, responses will go back through our egress proxy. Latency there could add 50–200ms unpredictably. How do you isolate model latency?
[08:16] Leo: We'll emit timestamps at the model runtime boundary in the host and in the client. That gives you both model-only TTFT and end-to-end TTFT. We'll include a delta analysis to attribute tail to network vs model.

[08:42] Sofia: Can we run a 2-day pilot with real traffic where Redwood deploys in our VPC?
[08:47] Maya: Yes — that's our suggested final validation. It requires peering and an access window, but it's the best way to validate p99 under real conditions.

[09:10] Mei: Quick question on batching configuration — do you test dynamic batching vs fixed windows?
[09:16] Leo: We'll test both. Dynamic batching is generally better for cost but can introduce variable TTFT depending on queueing. We'll show both latency and cost curves.

[09:40] Maya: Documentation handoffs: we'll share the POC playbook, security pack, and the measurement template after the call.

[10:05] Sofia: For the measurement template, can you add a column for business impact mapping? E.g., what percent of user flows would see >100ms regression.
[10:13] Maya: Yes, we'll add a user-impact mapping section.

[10:30] Leo: One operational note: for the replay harness we need to mask PII. If you can't share raw traces we support a telemetry-forward approach where we ingest a small telemetry-only sample and stitch synthetic payloads. That takes longer, though.

[10:52] Raj: We'll try to provide anonymized traces. I'll talk to security.

[11:05] Sofia: Let's discuss acceptance gating: do we need to meet SLOs for both baseline and peak slices?
[11:11] Maya: We propose baseline slice as the primary acceptance target and peak slice as a conditional target — if peak misses we want a mitigation plan (e.g., dedicated pool, different routing). We'll document fallback policies.

[11:32] Leo: Regarding model variants, for the POC we'll run two branches: quantized faster branch for cost/TPOT comparison and full precision for quality. Acceptance can be tiered — core endpoints must meet baseline SLOs on the chosen variant.

[12:02] Mei: About sampling windows — should we sample across weekdays and weekends? Our traffic pattern differs.
[12:08] Leo: Capture 2–3 weekdays plus at least one weekend slice if you have significant weekend usage. We'll prioritize the highest-volume windows for p99 stability.

[12:30] Maya: Timing check: we'll prepare the measurement sheet and scripts by Monday 2026-04-27, SE smoke run on 2026-04-25, and target the replay week of 2026-05-04. Does that align?
[12:44] Sofia: Yes. One ask — include a simple table showing estimated infra footprint for the pilot (GPU type/count) and cost ballpark.
[12:52] Leo: We'll include RTX-6000-like and A100 options with cost per hour. Also quantization impacts.

[13:10] Raj: Can Redwood run a quick 10k request TTFT vs TPOT microbenchmark now just to give us an initial baseline?
[13:16] Maya: Leo, can we commit to a 10k smoke?
[13:18] Leo: Yes, I'll run that on our side and post the results to the shared drive.

[13:30] Sofia: For the final acceptance report, we want: raw traces, percentile tables, cost breakdown, and a short executive summary.
[13:38] Maya: We'll deliver that.

[13:55] Leo: A few gotchas we've seen: KV cache warming can make early requests much faster — during replay, ensure prefix warm-up matches production; otherwise TTFT looks artificially good.
[14:07] Sofia: Good call. We'll annotate traces for sessions that should pre-warm.

[14:30] Mei: For the end-to-end pilot, what's the rollback plan if we see increased error rates?
[14:36] Maya: We'll maintain a canary and an automatic fallback to hosted model variant or previous model. We'll include a playbook.

[14:58] Raj: Any compliance work required for a Private deployment?
[15:03] Maya: We have an enterprise onboarding checklist — we'll share the SOC2 report, ISO summary, and the options for keeping logs in your account.

[15:25] Leo: On instrumentation again — token-level timestamps add overhead; we can sample token-level traces for 1% of requests if you want to bound storage.
[15:35] Sofia: Do that; full trace for 10% and token-level sampling for 1% sounds fine.

[15:55] Maya: Recap of key acceptance criteria: short-chat TTFT p95 <=250ms p99<=600ms on baseline; long-form per-token p95<=30ms p99<=60ms; error rate within 2%; cost within agreed delta. We'll put those in the POC charter.

[16:18] Leo: Next steps summary: Redwood shares measurement sheet & scripts (2026-04-27), run 10k smoke (2026-04-25), HelioHealth provides anonymized traces (2026-04-28), schedule replay week (target 2026-05-04).

[16:35] Raj: I'll escalate VPC peering.
[16:40] Sofia: We'll assemble the 200-eval prompt set and the sampling windows.

[16:50] Maya: Anything else?
[16:53] Mei: One last thing — could the report include a short appendix on sensitivity to batch size and queueing delay?
[16:58] Leo: Yes, that'll be a standard section.

[17:10] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up over email with the artifacts and calendar invites.

[57:30] (wrap) Maya: End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional word substitutions and filler; speaker labels approximate.
